papers.title_in_file: QUANTUM IN PRODUCTION: OPTIMIZING E-COMMERCE LOGISTICS (CASE STORY)
papers.what_it_is: A D-Wave marketing case story describing how the Pattison Food Group used D-Wave technology to automate weekly delivery driver scheduling, with reported time savings and deployment date.

assertions.value: The paper reports that the auto-scheduler cut a weekly task from 80 hours to 15 hours, which it states as an 80% time savings, and that it was deployed into production in late 2022.
assertions.anchor: Page 1, paragraph beginning 'The auto-scheduler is saving'; repeated on page 2
quotes: trimming what was once an 80-hour task to just 15 hours each week, an 80% time savings.
It was deployed into production in late 2022.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor case story reports a customer's figures with no method, baseline definition or measurement shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The savings from 80 to 15 hours is 65 hours, which is about 81 percent, so the stated 80 percent is a rounded figure. The paper gives no measurement method or comparison against a classical scheduler.

assertions.value: The paper states that driver schedules were built manually by a team of three to four e-commerce driver schedulers, and that this accounts for 80 person-hours of work each week.
quotes: Until recently, managing the driver schedules for those orders was a manual task.
a team of three to four e-commerce driver schedulers that creates schedules for all drivers, all across the provinces,
This accounts for 80 person-hours of work to build out the schedule for each week.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement by a company manager relayed in a vendor case story; no records are shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The only baseline is the previous manual process. The paper does not compare the quantum approach with a classical optimization solver.

assertions.value: The paper describes PFG as the largest purveyor of food and healthcare products in western Canada, with more than 100 retail locations offering online ordering.
quotes: PFG is the largest purveyor of food and healthcare products in western Canada, with more than 100 retail locations offering online ordering.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of the customer in a vendor document.

assertions.value: The paper reports that success was measured against a threshold of 95% of e-commerce shopper demand and against drivers receiving schedules that meet their expectations, and that Wai says each of the 100+ stores offering online ordering consistently meets these objectives.
quotes: Success was measured by a number of metrics, which included the ability to meet a threshold of 95% of the demand from the company’s e-commerce shoppers
each of the 100+ stores offering online ordering are consistently meeting these objectives.
assertions.certainty_reason: An interviewee's statement in a vendor case story; the paper shows no measured data per store.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say how the demand coverage or driver expectations were measured, or what the values were before the auto-scheduler.

assertions.value: The paper lists scheduling factors the system must handle, including which stores a driver is willing and able to get to, how many drivers each shift needs, and a minimum of 10 hours between shifts, and states that the number of variables and constraints adds to the complexity.
assertions.anchor: Page 1, paragraphs 5 and 6 (the list continues across the page break)
quotes: which stores a given driver is willing and able to get to, how many drivers are needed on each shift,
ensure that time between each shift is at least 10 hours, and other considerations.
The number of variables and constraints contribute to the complexity of developing optimal schedules.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of the problem it set out to solve.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no formulation, variable count or constraint count, so problem size cannot be judged from it.

assertions.value: The paper states the goal of the auto-scheduler as assigning each driver a weekly work assignment under user-designated constraints, so that each team member can work as many or as few shifts as they wish in a convenient and familiar location.
quotes: The auto-scheduler made it possible to assign drivers a weekly work assignment taking into account all manner of user-designated constraints,
each team member could work as many or as few shifts as they wish while operating in a convenient and familiar location.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of what the application is meant to do.

assertions.value: The paper states that after the problems were mathematically formulated, the PFG team built a computational pipeline that enabled the D-Wave platform to formulate an effective autoscheduling solution.
quotes: Once these problems were mathematically formulated, the PFG team built out a computational pipeline that enabled the D-Wave platform to formulate an effective autoscheduling solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of how its platform was used, with no technical detail.
assertions.reader_inference: The text names no solver type (for example annealing or hybrid), no problem formulation, no qubit or variable counts, no run times and no solution quality measures. The quantum contribution to the savings cannot be separated from the effect of automating a manual task.

assertions.value: The paper states that in the early days of the pandemic PFG began exploring quantum computing to automate shift-scheduling at individual stores, and that success with this initial test inspired the company to automate shift assignments for every driver in their fleet.
quotes: In the early days of the pandemic, the company began exploring the use of quantum computing to automate shift-scheduling tasks at individual stores.
inspired the company to address the more challenging goal of automating shift assignments for every driver in their fleet.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's account of the customer's project history; no results of the initial test are shown.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing Wai, that the remaining time spent is mainly due to a legacy workforce management system that still requires manual data-entry and is due for replacement, and that some manual oversight remains helpful for last-minute changes and requests such as unexpected sick time or recent turnover.
quotes: The remaining time expenditure, according to Wai, is principally due to the reliance on a legacy workforce management system, which still requires manual data-entry and is due for replacement.
some level of manual oversight is helpful in terms of dealing with last-minute changes and requests, such as unexpected sick time or recent turnover in the workforce.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit on the automation itself, on page 2.
assertions.reader_inference: The deployed system is not fully automatic: data entry is manual and humans handle late changes.

assertions.value: The paper gives a Calgary North example in a figure whose caption states that each schedule is based on an area that covers 1 or more stores, and that the maximum and minimum number of shifts are respected.
assertions.anchor: Figure caption, page 2 (the figure itself is an image)
quotes: CALGARY NORTH EXAMPLE: Each schedule is based on an area that covers 1 or more stores. Max and Min number of shifts as well as TM is respected.
assertions.certainty_reason: A caption only; the figure content is an image not carried by the text layer, and 'TM' is not defined in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: A schedule covers an area, not a single store, so the problem is solved per area. The abbreviation TM is not defined in the text layer.

assertions.value: The paper states that PFG is now looking at using the technology for workforce scheduling across all 300-plus stores in Canada and the United States, and quotes Wai saying that problem is very large but that he is confident his team will be able to solve it.
quotes: optimizing workforce scheduling across all 300-plus stores in Canada and the United States.
“That problem is very large,” says Wai.
assertions.certainty_reason: A stated intention and a statement of confidence, not a result.
assertions.reader_inference: The larger problem is stated as a goal and open challenge, not as something demonstrated.

assertions.value: The paper defines an in-production quantum application as one where the business has gone through the quantum journey from use case exploration and identification, to validation, POC and pilot, all the way to deploying a real-world application that is delivering ROI-driving business outcomes.
quotes: An “in-production” quantum application means that the business has gone through the quantum journey
from use case exploration and identification, to validation, POC and pilot, all the way to deploying a real-world application
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the term, given in its opening paragraph.
assertions.reader_inference: The definition is the vendor's own and does not require a quantum speedup or an advantage over classical methods.

assertions.value: The paper claims that the first commercial quantum applications in production are using D-Wave's quantum technology.
quotes: The first commercial quantum applications in production are using D-Wave’s quantum technology.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's priority claim about itself, with no evidence given in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim depends on the paper's own definition of 'in production' and is not checked against other vendors.
